key_points: T. H. Chowdary's cover feature indicts government primary and secondary education in Andhra Pradesh as collapsed and captured by teacher unions, proposing school vouchers, deregulation of private-school fees, English-medium instruction from Class VI, and a 'Self Employed Teacher' scheme paying villagers per pupil who passes exams.

Kuldip Nayar's "When Awards are Rewards" and Kashinath Divecha's "Dump Devalued Government Awards" both attack the Bharat Ratna/Padma honours system as a politically arbitrary process that violates the Constitution's spirit, with Divecha calling for the awards to be abolished altogether and merit recognition left to peers and civil society.

H. R. Bapu Satyanarayana's essay on Raj Thackeray situates the anti-North-Indian backlash in Mumbai within a wider pattern of regional chauvinism, arguing Raj is replicating his uncle Bal Thackeray's earlier tactics against South Indians and suggesting the Congress-led UPA may be tacitly tolerating the affair for electoral advantage.

Ashok Karnik's "Point Counter Point" argues both sides of the Tata Nano's launch, the Sino-Indian 'Vision Document' signed during the Prime Minister's China visit, and the Mumbai New Year molestation case.

Arvind A.'s "Bhutto and Pakistan: Quo Vadis India?" warns that Pakistan's post-assassination instability, combined with its nuclear and possibly chemical or biological weapons capability, poses a serious risk to India, surveying its history of military rule and US arms sales.

Firoze Hirjikaka's "Cornucopia" criticises Mayawati for suspending IAS officers who praised Rahul Gandhi, comparing her cultivation of blind loyalty to Hitler's rise, and separately condemns Parsi religious leaders for trying to block a lecture advocating admission of outsiders to Zoroastrianism.

An unsigned report covers the Indian Liberal Group's Fourth National Convention in Chennai, where N. Vittal delivered the inaugural address and delegates adopted resolutions on economic reform, national security, coalition governance, and environmental conservation.

Suman Oak's "Rites, Rituals and Festivals" instalment on Mahashivaraatri traces the festival's mythological origins and ritual practice, and Tenzin Tsundue announces a six-month 'Long March to Freedom' from Dharamsala modelled on Gandhi's Salt March, timed to draw attention around the Beijing Olympics.

Two book reviews cover Mahendra Lawoti's edited volume on contentious politics and democratisation in Nepal and Ashok K. Mehta's study of the Royal Nepal Army's flawed counter-insurgency effort against the Maoists.

The unsigned front-page editorial "Tibet Will Be Free" compares the 2008 Tibetan unrest to the unforeseen collapse of Soviet hegemony after 1989, accuses China of demographic engineering through Han resettlement, and reaffirms the magazine's own 1959 editorial pledge of solidarity with Tibetans.

An unsigned tribute marks the death of Justice H. R. Khanna, recalling his lone dissent in the 1976 ADM Jabalpur case upholding habeas corpus rights during the Emergency, his resulting supersession for the Chief Justiceship, and his authorship of the Constitution's 'basic structure' doctrine.

Mohan Dharia and M. D. Kini both examine the Raj Thackeray-Abu Azmi migrant confrontation as a symptom of Maharashtra's governance failure rather than migrant opportunism, tracing the state's decline from Y. B. Chavan's era and calling for decentralised rural development and respect for citizens' constitutional right to migrate freely.

Kunwar Sinha argues for a formal UK-style Code of Advertising for Indian television, contrasting India's unregulated ad-saturated broadcasting, including on Doordarshan, with Britain's Advertising Standards Authority and Ofcom regime.

Ashok Karnik's "Point Counter Point" debates the Thackeray-driven Mumbai backlash, the spread of corruption following the Dr. Horror kidney-transplant scandal, and the significance of Pakistan's 2008 elections.

Firoze Hirjikaka's "Cornucopia" criticises Indian media for amplifying fringe protest groups such as the Rajput Karni Sena over the film 'Jodha Akbar,' and faults state governments for letting such groups dictate terms, drawing a parallel to the MNS's anti-migrant violence.

An unsigned piece offers a skeptical view of Obama-mania in the US primaries, questioning his foreign-policy readiness, alongside Taslima Nasreen's first-person account of months of confinement and pressure to leave India.

Suman Oak's "Rites, Rituals and Festivals" instalment on Holi traces its mythological origins and proposes ecological reforms to the bonfire tradition, while an obituary remembers Radical Humanist thinker Sibnarayan Ray, a close associate of M. N. Roy's movement.

R. Srinivasan's piece on the death of General Suharto brands him a 'kleptomaniac and mass murderer' responsible for hundreds of thousands of killings and decades of family enrichment, comparing his impunity to Pinochet, Stroessner, and Pol Pot, while Prof. V. C. Phadke reviews a book on the 1930 Chirner Jungle Satyagraha.

N. Vittal's "Roots of Indian Democracy" credits India's 60-year democratic survival to a pluralist constitutional culture and resilient institutions tested by the Emergency, then uses the Nandigram SEZ controversy to warn that short-term political calculation is letting Naxalite 'revolutionary zones' expand unchecked.

Ashok Sahu traces the Communist Party of India (Maoist)'s formation from the 2004 merger of the People's War Group and Maoist Communist Centre back to the 1948 Telangana uprising and 1967 Naxalbari revolt, detailing its roughly 9,000-9,500 cadres across 192 districts and its goal of a contiguous 'Compact Revolutionary Zone' from Nepal to Andhra Pradesh.

Col. T. S. Tanwar surveys insurgency across the seven North-Eastern states, tracing it to A. Z. Phizo's Naga National Council and citing 24 active insurgent groups, and attributes the unrest to shared economic backwardness and central neglect.

V. Balachandran's essay rejects the idea that strong armies or policing alone guarantee security, applying a RAND Corporation framework on 'ungoverned territories' to India's Maoist-affected districts and calling for the Centre to assert a clearer legal right to intervene in state security crises.

E. D'Souza examines the Indian Army's shortage of over 11,200 officers, attributing it to private-sector pay competition and quoting senior generals on the unattractiveness of military careers, while flagging conscription as a discussed but rejected remedy.

S. C. Sharma argues that coercive interrogation of terrorism suspects, though ethically fraught, has in specific historical cases (Aldo Moro, a 1995 Philippines plot, IRA suspects in Northern Ireland) prevented greater harm, and contends extending POW protections to terrorists is misguided.
The issue opens with Tenzin Tsundue's account of the 2008 Delhi leg of the Olympic torch relay and the security clampdown on Tibetan protesters.

Major General Eustace D'Souza and Capt. J. N. Choppra both protest the Sixth Pay Commission's treatment of the Armed Forces, describing unprecedented unity among all three Service Chiefs and 30 War Memorial protests, and calling for a dedicated Services Pay Commission and one-rank-one-pension.

V. Balachandran concludes his four-part national security series by using William Sleeman's colonial-era suppression of the Thuggee networks as a model for a proposed federal police force to handle terrorism, Naxalism, and trans-border crime.
Ashok Karnik's "Point Counter Point" debates a Beijing Olympics boycott over Tibet, IPL cheerleaders as 'moral policing,' and the Animal Welfare Board's regulation of advertising.

Dr. P. M. Kamath's essay on globalisation, drawing on Alan Greenspan's memoir, argues globalisation is reshaping economics, politics and even terrorism financing, while criticising Indian Marxists for inconsistency on foreign economic engagement.
Firoze Hirjikaka's "Cornucopia" argues a Beijing Olympics boycott would be counterproductive and condemns Raj Thackeray's demand to ban non-Marathi festivals in Maharashtra as dictatorial overreach.

Kusum Choppra's "Points to Ponder" criticises TRP-driven media coverage of a cricketer's slap incident over the Pay Commission's treatment of soldiers, and questions renewed US interest in Afghanistan as a pattern of resource extraction.

Sharad Bailur reviews Francis Fukuyama's 'Our Posthuman Future,' arguing Fukuyama overstates biotechnology's political dangers while underestimating the more radical, imminent transformations from nanotechnology.

Brief tributes mark the deaths of playwright Vijay Tendulkar, remembered for fearless works like 'Sakharam Binder,' and political science teacher Prof. S. V. Kogekar, while G. D. Karve contributes a nostalgic letter about his 1955-56 posting in Trivandrum.

Sunil Bhandare and C. S. Deshpande's cover feature argues the mid-2008 inflation spike to a 13-year high of about 11% is a global, oil-driven phenomenon rather than a consequence of India's post-1991 liberalisation, tracing repeated double-digit inflation under pre-reform centralised planning and warning against a return to price controls.

Ashok Karnik's "Point Counter Point" debates whether inflation caused the BJP's Karnataka victory, the feasibility of a Congress-BJP coalition, and India's response to the May 2008 Jaipur bomb blasts.

V. Balachandran profiles John McCain and Barack Obama ahead of the 2008 US election, contrasting McCain's hawkish 'Jacksonian' foreign policy with Obama's stated philosophy of 'empathy and inclusiveness.'

Eknaath Nagarkar's allegorical essay personifies Indian democracy as a vulnerable 'damsel,' tracing its history from Nehru's choice of secularism through the Emergency to the Karnataka forest brigand Veerappan as a decades-long antagonist of the state.

Firoze Hirjikaka's "Cornucopia" criticises politicians' selective outrage over a minister's inverted flag-hoisting, cites nine major terror bombings since 2005 to argue security agencies rarely act on intelligence in time, and satirises the Shiv Sena's Bombay-to-Mumbai renaming campaign.
The "Many Voices" digest compiles press quotations from April-June 2008 on topics including Advani's book on Benazir Bhutto, caste politics, globalisation, Tibet, and Taslima Nasreen's exile.

Sharad Bailur's lead article traces India's nuclear-policy history from Nehru through Shastri, Indira Gandhi's Pokhran I, and Vajpayee's Pokhran II to defend Manmohan Singh's US nuclear deal as necessary for uranium supply, mocking the opportunistic 'fishing in a horse trough' opposition from the BJP, Left, and Mayawati.

Major General Eustace D'Souza's tribute to Field Marshal Sam Manekshaw, who died in June 2008, recounts his wounding at Sittang Bridge, his role planning the 1971 victory over Pakistan, and calls for a posthumous Bharat Ratna while criticising officials for skipping his funeral; a reprinted Ardeshir Cowasjee column from Dawn adds his wartime friendship with Yahya Khan.

Ashok Karnik's "Point Counter Point" debates the nuclear deal and Manmohan Singh's confidence vote, the Deoband fatwa against jihadist violence, and Congress infighting disrupting a Sonia Gandhi rally in Maharashtra.

Sanjeev Sabhlok's debut column, "Come On Liberals: Let's Change India!", announces the Freedom Team of India initiative to recruit about 1,500 citizen-leaders to eventually contest elections on a platform of freedom and anti-corruption.

Firoze Hirjikaka's "Cornucopia" criticises Bal Thackeray's Saamna editorial calling for Hindu suicide bombers after the Mumbai theatre blasts, and blames poorly run municipal schools for driving Mumbai's slum families toward illegal unregistered schools.

A report covers the June 2008 transfer of Amarnath Shrine land triggering Kashmir Valley protests and the collapse of the Congress-PDP coalition government, and another covers a government order mandating SC/ST/OBC faculty reservations at the IITs over the objections of IIT directors.

R. Srinivasan reviews Vinay Lal's 'Empire of Knowledge,' which argues the UN and international financial institutions function as extensions of American power and casts Gandhi as an indigenous alternative to Western development models.

An unsigned piece on media trivialisation uses the Aarushi murder coverage to show political news share on Hindi TV channels falling sharply between 2005 and 2007, and a short piece marks Nelson Mandela's 90th birthday.

Ashok Karnik's "A Sleeping Behemoth" surveys three decades of terrorism in India from the Khalistan insurgency to 2008 jihadi attacks, arguing government inertia and lack of accountability, not resource shortfalls, are to blame, and defends harsher anti-terror laws like TADA and POTA.

V. Balachandran's companion essay, "A Case of Abdication of Responsibility," argues the Ministry of Home Affairs and state governments have ignored the 2001 post-Kargil Group of Ministers report for seven years, and again invokes William Sleeman's suppression of Thuggee as a model for a proposed federal anti-terrorism agency.

Ashok Karnik's "Point Counter Point" debates the Manmohan Singh government's survival of the July 2008 confidence vote, the recurring 2008 bomb blasts in Jaipur, Bangalore, and Ahmedabad, and the right to privacy after the Aarushi Talwar case.
B. Ramesh Babu reports from Washington on a lull in the 2008 US presidential race, covering Obama's foreign tour, the John Edwards scandal, and race as an undercurrent in the campaign.

R. Srinivasan marks the centenary of Lokmanya Tilak's 1908 sedition trial and transportation to Mandalay, detailing the flawed, communally split jury verdict and Chief Justice M. C. Chagla's 1956 plaque acknowledging the injustice.
Sanjeev Sabhlok's second column promotes the Freedom Team of India, aiming to recruit 1,500 citizen-leaders by 2014, arguing freedom has benefited the poor more than any alternative economic system.

Sadanand B. Kumta critiques the Sixth Pay Commission's 40% salary hike for central government employees as rewarding an unaccountable bureaucracy, while Firoze Hirjikaka's "Cornucopia" questions whether India's democracy genuinely serves its people and laments the muted public response to Sam Manekshaw's funeral.

A book review covers Tan Tai Yong's 'The Garrison State' on the militarisation of colonial Punjab under the 'martial races' doctrine, and reader letters address the Savitri-Satyavan legend and the fallout of the July 2008 no-confidence motion.

R. Srinivasan's cover essay surveys India's escalating civil conflicts in late 2008 -- Naxalite control over roughly a third of the country's land mass, anti-Christian violence in Orissa and Karnataka blamed on the VHP and Bajrang Dal, and Bodo-Muslim violence in Assam linked to illegal immigration -- and argues the state is abdicating its duty to maintain law and order.

Sharad Bailur's "Lucky Again!" argues India's post-Independence survival has depended more on fortuitous timing of leaders like Gandhi, Patel, and Nehru than on policy foresight, and warns that reliance on luck cannot continue without institutional reform.

Ashok Karnik's "Point Counter Point" debates whether Union Home Minister Shivraj Patil should be held responsible for a wave of bombings, the government's contradictory anti-terror messaging, and the Labour Minister's advisory to industry after the Noida lynching of an Italian CEO.

Sanjeev Sabhlok's column argues for radically decentralised urban governance, proposing small, accountable local councils modelled on New York and Melbourne to replace India's unaccountable 'mega-municipalities.'
Prem Vaidya argues for abolishing India's colonial-era film censorship regime, tracing its history and citing the double standard between strict cinema censorship and unregulated television content.

M. D. Kini argues India lacks the ambition to pursue available energy and water solutions, citing Anand Mahindra's critique of India's timid solar policy and comparing it unfavourably to the ambition behind the Green Revolution and nuclear programme.

Firoze Hirjikaka's "Cornucopia" argues the Parsi community's scandal-ridden 2008 Panchayat elections and internal infighting, not external conversion pressure, are the real threat to its survival, and a companion piece describes routine diversion of relief and subsidy schemes to politically connected beneficiaries.

Xerxes Desai's parody of Auden's "September 1, 1939" recasts the poem's warning about the outbreak of World War II onto the 2008 global financial crisis, and Ashok Karnik reviews Ajay Darshan Behera's 'Violence, Terrorism and Human Security in South Asia.'

Ajit Karnik defends the liberal 'State and markets' position against both market fundamentalism and the Left's opportunistic revival of anti-capitalist rhetoric after the 2008 financial crisis, invoking Hayek's 'Fatal Conceit' against the assumption that government is omniscient.

B. Ramesh Babu reads Barack Obama's election as a historic, values-affirming landslide reflecting demographic change and a repudiation of the Bush era, while Nitin Raut counters that Obama's foreign-policy room for manoeuvre toward India, Pakistan and China is more constrained than the euphoria suggests.

Ashok Karnik's "Point Counter Point" debates 'Hindu terrorism' after the Malegaon blasts arrests, the Maharashtra Navnirman Sena's attacks on non-Maharashtrians, and whether Obama's win holds lessons for Indian politics.

Vice Admiral (retd.) I. C. Rao reports on the surge of Somali piracy in the Gulf of Aden, describing the Indian Navy's rescue of the Jag Arnav and the prolonged hijacking of the Stolt Valor, and calls for an international naval task force under the IMO.

Sanjeev Sabhlok argues Indian property rights have been progressively eroded since independence through Nehru's land ceiling laws and the 1971 and 1978 constitutional amendments, and proposes a framework for legitimate compulsory land acquisition based on local referenda and expert compensation panels.

Suman Oak's "Rites, Rituals and Festivals" instalment on Tulsi Vivah recounts competing Puranic origin myths and criticises the ritual as ideologically designed to confine women to domestic servitude.

Firoze Hirjikaka's "Cornucopia" uses the Jet Airways mass-sacking-and-reinstatement episode to argue Indians want free-market rewards without accepting free-market risk, and praises Ratan Tata's withdrawal from the Singur Nano project as pushback against political interference.

Reader letters address Naxalism and religious conversion, the razing of a Sardar Patel statue in Uttar Pradesh, and the 123 Agreement/Hyde Act debate, while the editor's note previews the magazine's landmark 500th issue.

Jagdeep S. Chhokar argues Indian democracy is at a critical juncture after 26/11, tracing the erosion of political morality since the 1951 H. G. Mudgal case to an estimated 100-120 sitting MPs facing criminal cases, and urges citizens to register, vote informed, and use the Rule 49-O protest vote absent a 'None of the Above' option.

A. K. Venkat Subramanian details his years-long campaign, via PIL and the Election Commission, to popularise Rule 49-O and add a 'None of the Above' button to EVMs, citing rising Tamil Nadu turnout after voter-awareness drives.

Ashok Karnik's post-mortem of the 26/11 attacks describes a ten-man force holding Mumbai hostage for 60 hours despite prior IB and RAW warnings, criticises sensationalist media coverage and Pakistan's denials, and calls for citizen accountability rather than complacency.

V. Balachandran argues India remains a 'soft state' that has never substantively reformed its colonial-era intelligence apparatus, contrasting its lack of a codified legal mandate with intelligence services in the US, UK, Canada, Australia, and South Africa.

R. C. A. Godbole reflects on the burning of the Taj Palace Hotel, highlighting informal mutual-aid networks among Mumbai commuters during the crisis and proposing a public collection to fund the hotel's rebuilding as a gesture of civic solidarity.

Vivek Raju surveys candidate explanations for the 26/11 attack -- incompetent governance, harbouring states, financiers, arms suppliers, religious ideology -- and argues ending terrorism would require a near-impossible level of global coordination against the arms trade.

The editorial 'Of Cabbages and Kings' criticises commuters who vandalised railway property during a Mumbai motormen's strike and compares Zimbabwe's cholera crisis and North Korea as examples of governmental failure enabling harm to citizens.

The 500th-issue editorial dedicates the anthology to readers and supporters, explaining that fewer than forty articles were selected from fifty-six years of publication, spanning the magazine's June 1952 founding to 2009, with a six-month gap during the 1975 Emergency.

"The Evolution of Freedom First" traces the magazine's origins to post-independence India's socialist planning and admiration for the Soviet Union, describing its 1952 launch as a defence of cultural freedom and a liberal alternative built on free enterprise, secular values, and intellectual openness.

The reprinted 1952 statement "The Open Society" defines the magazine's founding purpose as resisting the drift from personal responsibility into authoritarian security, arguing that dissent and open debate are necessary to truth and social progress.

Minoo Masani's "Rededication" renews the magazine's founding commitment to open debate against what he calls a Marxist counter-revolution, citing Jayaprakash Narayan's criticism of the 25th Amendment and warning that press freedom is endangered.

"A Tiff with the Establishment" answers Prime Minister Nehru's parliamentary criticism of the Indian Committee for Cultural Freedom and Democratic Research Service as political fronts, defending both as independent bodies and invoking the Hungarian uprising to justify their anti-Soviet stance.

R. A. Jahagirdar's "Mill 'On Liberty'" marks the 150th anniversary of Mill's book, sketching its harm principle and defence of individuality while noting later criticisms by James Fitzjames Stephen and H. L. A. Hart.

Jayaprakash Narayan's reprinted "Incentives to Goodness" argues, from the standpoint of a former devotee of dialectical materialism, that social reconstruction is impossible without a corresponding individual moral reconstruction, since materialism cannot supply a rational reason to be good.

R. Srinivasan's bicentenary essay on Darwin situates him alongside Marx and Freud as a shaper of modern thought, explaining natural selection and tracing public controversies over evolution from the Huxley-Wilberforce exchange to the Scopes trial.

A. D. Moddie argues the 2008 global financial crisis has shaken the twentieth century's major economic ideologies -- Soviet communism, state socialism, Chinese pragmatism, and American capitalism -- and calls for pragmatic new institutions and a shift from Atlantic to Pacific economic power.

Ashok Karnik's "Point Counter Point" weighs police courage during 26/11 against systemic failures, welcomes the new National Investigation Agency while warning that inter-agency turf protection remains the harder problem, and argues courts and voters must prevent convicted candidates from normalising criminality in politics.

Sadanand B. Kumte shifts blame for 26/11 from politicians to the permanent bureaucracy, arguing bureaucrats hide behind procedure and status while escaping accountability for security and administrative failures.

P. R. Dubhashi urges India not to read Barack Obama's presidency narrowly through Kashmir, CTBT, and NPT anxieties, welcoming a prospective shift from Bush-era unilateralism toward diplomacy and multilateralism.

Sharu S. Rangnekar frames terrorism as an extreme, learned form of group prejudice rather than a product of any one religion or education level, arguing cosmopolitan interaction and counter-propaganda can convert prejudice into tolerance.

Firoze Hirjikaka's "Cornucopia" defends the constitutional obligation to provide Ajmal Kasab a legal defence, argues India's post-26/11 diplomatic ambiguity toward Pakistan usefully preserves American pressure, and reads the murder of Paloma Fernandes as a symptom of instant-gratification culture.

B. Leela profiles Justice Nitoor Srinivasa Rau as a Gandhian liberal humanist whose Kannada publishing work, nationalist activity, and legal career culminated in his role as India's first Central Vigilance Commissioner, while Sanjeev Sabhlok argues Indian liberals should overcome myths about electoral violence and cost to enter organised politics.

Surjit Singh presents the Jantar Mantar veterans' agitation as a fight for 'izzat' as much as pension arrears, citing the denial of One Rank One Pension and Sixth Pay Commission anomalies as evidence of a systematic downgrading of military status by civilian bureaucracy.

Sharad Bailur argues Pakistan has repeatedly defined its national identity in opposition to India rather than as an independent project, tracing this from Partition through the 1971 war, nuclear rivalry, and discomfort with the 'AfPak' label, including a courteous email exchange with retired Air Vice Marshal Shahzad Chaudhry.

Firoze Hirjikaka's essay attacks India's political class for opportunism and institutional manipulation, moving from Narendra Modi and media regulation through police reform, Bilkis Bano, Mayawati, and Sadhvi Pragya, while noting early signs of accountability through the Right to Information Act.

Ashok Karnik's "Point Counter Point" describes the 2009 election as an auction of loyalty among wealthy candidates, criticises the mishandling of Varun Gandhi's Pilibhit speech, and reads the Lahore Police Training Centre attack as evidence of Pakistan's unresolved Taliban problem.

H. R. Bapu Satyanarayana criticises politically useful labels such as calling Mangalore 'Talibanised' or branding the BJP as non-secular, arguing Congress's inherited legitimacy from the freedom struggle let it define secularism against its rivals.

Sanjeev Sabhlok develops equal opportunity as a liberal doctrine distinct from equal outcomes, aligning with Hayek on a social minimum funded only after defence, police, and justice, and proposing school vouchers, health insurance vouchers, and a negative income tax.

B. K. Karanjia's profile of Rustom Masani, part of the "Profiles of Indian Liberals" series, presents him as a mediator between Congress and British authorities who criticised the 1939 Congress ministries' resignation and mourned Partition's costs.

Derek Humphry's manifesto argues for a competent adult's right to choose death amid terminal suffering, and Nitin G. Raut's essay on Israel at sixty praises its parliamentary democracy, kibbutz-based social integration, and agricultural self-sufficiency.

V. Krishna Moorthy surveys global tax havens and post-2008 pressure on Swiss banking secrecy, linking Indian black money to under-invoicing, kickbacks, hawala, and the licence-permit raj, and urges the new post-2009-election government to pursue illicit funds abroad.

Sharad Bailur pushes back against campaign rhetoric promising quick recovery of black money from Swiss banks, arguing Swiss confidentiality and the likely complicity of politicians across parties make such promises implausible.

Ashok Karnik's "Point Counter Point" reads Mumbai's low post-26/11 voter turnout as civic failure, questions whether coalition parties will prioritise national interest over power, and warns India against letting US-Pakistan dynamics dictate its military strategy toward the Taliban.

M. A. Haque argues madrasas proliferate not chiefly from foreign funding or communal politics but from social isolation, poor access to mainstream education, and sustaining religious donation channels like zakat and waqf, and calls for Muslim children to have a genuine choice between madrasa and mainstream schooling.

Firoze Hirjikaka's "Cornucopia" argues Narendra Modi's national ambitions are premature given his Gujarat-bound charisma and the shadow of Godhra, and separately laments the decline of circulating libraries and serious reading culture in South Mumbai.

Sanjeev Sabhlok argues Indian political corruption is structurally produced by election-finance rules that force costly campaigns underground, proposing abolition of expenditure limits, audited accounts, and higher legislator pay as remedies.

S. Radhakrishnan and R. Uppili use the Satyam-Maytas scandal to illustrate crony capitalism, contrasting it with small enterprises like Mumbai's dabbawallahs, arguing the informal sector contributes 30-45% of GDP yet is excluded from formal bank credit.

An unsigned article condemns India's diplomatic silence over Aung San Suu Kyi's continued detention, and a companion tribute from S. V. Raju remembers Swatantra Party worker J. Ramabhadran, alongside P. L. Dash's opening piece on post-Soviet Central Asian geopolitics.

A tribute to Rajmata Gayatri Devi reprints her 1961 speech announcing she had joined the Swatantra Party, in which she criticises rising taxes, cooperative farming, nationalisation, and broken promises to former princely rulers while defending citizens' right to choose their political affiliation.

D. R. Pendse's budget essay argues the 2009-10 Union Budget signals a return to command-economy habits, criticising the narrow electoral-trust mechanism for political funding, the 6.8% fiscal deficit, and a ritualistic Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act that should be rescinded rather than ceremonially revived.

V. Balachandran argues the government's proposed Maoist surrender policy will fail because it mistakes an ideological and social insurgency for a simple criminal-incentive problem, citing exploitation, caste hierarchy, and neglected villages as the true sustaining causes, illustrated by the Gangapur case where a road and direct engagement weakened Naxalite influence.

Ashok Karnik's "Point Counter Point" is skeptical of US dependence on Pakistan under the AfPak policy, rebukes New York Times commentary urging India to concede more on trade and Kashmir, and criticises Indian media for magnifying national failures.

Sanjeev Sabhlok proposes a liberal policy for higher education in which the state exits ownership of institutions while retaining accreditation, selling public tertiary colleges and replacing subsidies with income-tax-linked loans for poor meritorious students.

E. D'Souza asks whether India risks repeating the 1962 war given renewed Chinese pressure around Tawang and NEFA, noting improved infrastructure and morale in Arunachal Pradesh but calling for stronger intelligence, logistics, and a Chief of Defence Staff.

Prasenjit Maiti's essay on women and war argues that rape and sexualised violence are used to humiliate enemy communities, moving from epic examples to modern atrocities including comfort women, Vietnam, and Abu Ghraib, and calls for security-force sensitisation.

Gopal Krishna Gandhi's review of the Uttankita Vidya Aranya epigraphy volume praises inscriptions as durable public communication and ancient equivalents of broadcasting, restoring primary sources to historical curiosity.

The cover feature by H. R. Bapu Satyanarayana uses Jaswant Singh's expulsion from the BJP over his Jinnah book to diagnose broader BJP disarray, arguing the real danger is the erosion of a credible opposition able to check entrenched Congress-family dominance.

K. Vedamurthy revisits C. Rajagopalachari's wartime attempts to negotiate with Jinnah and the Muslim League, arguing Rajaji's willingness to discuss Pakistan 'in principle' was strategic realism rather than surrender, drawing on Hiren Mukherjee, Rajmohan Gandhi, and Sri Aurobindo.

Keshav Rau argues the Gujarat ban on Jaswant Singh's Jinnah book exposes the danger of letting state governments ban books over partisan displeasure, proposing that book-ban powers be transferred to an independent authority appealable to the Supreme Court.

Ashok Karnik's "Point Counter Point" complicates partisan certainty on the reassessment of Jinnah, the RSS's ability to fix the BJP's problems, and the enduring lesson of the Kandahar hijacking as a failure of advance crisis planning.

P. R. Dubhashi argues Indian higher education has drifted from Nehru's humanistic ideal toward marketisation and credential competition, supporting expansion while warning that political patronage and fragmented regulation undermine both access and quality.

Sanjeev Sabhlok attacks foreign aid from a liberal standpoint, arguing it fuels corruption and dependency rather than removing poverty, and calls for it to be replaced by free trade, scholarships, and support for domestic liberal reformers.

Reader letters and the "Many Voices" page cover Shashi Tharoor's 'cattle class' remark, Mumbai voter apathy linked to the loss of local democratic control over civic decisions, and public panic about swine flu.

Admiral Arun Prakash's cover feature argues India's nuclear and strategic policy-making suffers from weak institutional checks and insufficient military input, tracing the problem to post-independence idealism and a long-standing separation between scientists and soldiers.

Ashok Karnik's "Point Counter Point" urges India to stand firm against Chinese pressure on Arunachal Pradesh, defends Shashi Tharoor's 'cattle class' remark as harmless banter, and argues Pakistan's denials over Kargil, 26/11, and proliferation have damaged its credibility.

Sharad Bailur rebuts an earlier warning about a "return of one-party dominance," arguing the 2009 Congress victory does not amount to dictatorship since the UPA remained a coalition dependent on allies, contrasting Congress's resilience in defeat with BJP triumphalism.

Keshav Rau examines Jaswant Singh's expulsion from the BJP over his Jinnah book, asking why Singh remained in a party whose positions clashed with his stated sympathy for Indian Muslims for decades, and criticises his retention of the Public Accounts Committee chairmanship after expulsion.

Firoze Hirjikaka's "Cornucopia" questions the source of politicians' disproportionate wealth, argues arresting Hafiz Saeed would not solve the structural threat from Pakistan's army and ISI, and defends newspapers as an indispensable civic habit.
Narendra Nayak discusses the S.V.S. College burkha controversy in Bantwal to examine tensions between individual dress freedom and secular uniformity in state-funded educational institutions.

Sanjeev Sabhlok begins a liberal theory of taxation, framing taxes as payment for public goods under a social contract and beginning to justify progressive taxation through price discrimination and unequal consumer surplus.

A tribute to rationalist B. Premanand remembers his village-to-village science demonstrations, his magazine Indian Skeptic, and his deathbed declaration rejecting rumours that illness had turned him toward religion.

Nitin G. Raut argues the October 2009 Assembly election results should not be read as a sweeping Congress mandate, attributing the Maharashtra victory partly to opposition fragmentation from the MNS split and faulting the BJP for weak leadership and opposition-for-opposition's-sake tactics.

Keshav Rau criticises Prime Minister Manmohan Singh's public comments giving a 'clean chit' during the 2G spectrum allocation investigation as undermining the independence of the CBI and Central Vigilance Commission.

H. R. Bapu Satyanarayana reads strikes, caste and regional unrest, Maoist violence, and corruption as symptoms of a deeper national disaffection produced by political degeneration and compromised institutions, while acknowledging India's agricultural, scientific, and military achievements.

Ashok Karnik's "Point Counter Point" weighs the Maharashtra election result against continuing MNS-style vote splitting and street violence, and dismisses Pakistani claims linking India to Taliban violence as domestic propaganda.

Giridhar Prabhu argues Indian political parties operate in ways hostile to constitutional democracy, calling for party constitutions to be reviewed against democratic norms and party resources separated from state resources.

Neelakant Patri examines Indian companies buying or leasing African farmland for food production, linking the trend to India's food-security concerns amid monsoon failure and pulse and sugar shortages.

Sanjeev Sabhlok's second part on liberal taxation argues for a broader tax base, less regressive taxation, and lower company taxes, while Firoze Hirjikaka's "Cornucopia" criticises the Maharashtra government's delayed air support for police during a Naxalite ambush in Gadchiroli.

The editor's "Between Ourselves" appeals for reader support amid rising production costs and thin revenue, proposing subscriptions, donations, and issue sponsorship to sustain the magazine as it enters its 58th year.

The cover feature on India-China relations opens with Maj. Gen. Eustace D'Souza's continuation of "Are We Heading for a 1962 Repeat," drawing on personal military encounters to argue India should hold firm through winter along the frontier while improving equipment and infrastructure.

Brig. S. C. Sharma surveys China's border disputes and regional strategy, portraying it as expansionist but pragmatic, using Pakistan, Myanmar, Sri Lanka, and Nepal to widen its influence and constrain India.

Ashok Karnik argues India should not read weakness into the government's public ambiguity toward China, welcoming firmness on the Dalai Lama's Tawang visit and warning against arguments that ask India to concede ground on Aksai Chin for the sake of appearing reasonable.

A recorded seminar "Discussions" section debates the McMahon Line, Panchsheel, Aksai Chin, and whether India should combine military deterrence with economic and soft-power projection against China, extending the rivalry to the Indian Ocean and Africa.

Nitin Pai's "Why Fixing Drains Will Help Counter Terrorism" argues counterterrorism cannot be separated from ordinary governance, rejecting both military retaliation and the idea that security agencies can function well while public works and policing remain weak.

Reader letters mix support for the magazine with warnings against political fasts used coercively, calls for Hindu-Muslim reconciliation following the Liberhan Report on Ayodhya, and proposals to bring voting facilities closer to voters.

Meera Sanyal's climate essay reads the Copenhagen summit's failure as less important than practical lessons India can draw from local climate action, proposing solar PV electrification of villages instead of abstract emissions formulas.

Sadanand B. Kumta reviews the Kyoto Protocol and Copenhagen accord, arguing the outcome left targets vague and effectively benefited the United States and China while leaving India's declared defence of developing-country interests outmanoeuvred.

Firoze Hirjikaka's essay on child suicides links youth despair and violence to academic pressure, consumption, peer pressure, and parental indulgence, calling for parents to restore the discipline of saying no.

Sunita, writing from Australia, challenges the framing of attacks on Indian students as simply racist, arguing that crime, precarious work, poor assimilation, and media amplification all complicate the picture following Nitin Garg's death.
R. C. Saxena attacks Gujarat's compulsory voting legislation as illiberal and coercive, arguing the Constitution creates neither a right nor a duty to vote.

Ashok Karnik's "Point Counter Point" weighs Copenhagen as either failure or pragmatic progress, debates the merits of creating new smaller states, and separates procurement concerns over bullet-proof jackets from the mistaken belief that equipment failure caused 26/11.

N. S. Venkataraman praises Sri Lanka's decision to hold a presidential election soon after its civil conflict as a sign of democratic confidence, while flagging unresolved concerns about press harassment and reassurance to Tamil civilians.
Nitin G. Raut criticises India's VIP culture through the Shah Rukh Khan airport-detention controversy, arguing legal equality and security should not be subordinated to celebrity status.

Ashok Karnik analyses the Pradhan Committee report on 26/11, praising its speed and integrity while criticising public fixation on leaked bullet-proof jacket files over the deeper failures in threat appreciation, coastal security, and intelligence handling.

Ashok Karnik presents and comments on Vice-President Hamid Ansari's case for democratic oversight of intelligence agencies, comparing oversight models in the US, UK, Norway, and Germany and using the Kargil Review Committee as evidence executive-only oversight is inadequate.

V. Balachandran welcomes Ansari's reform proposals but urges caution about parliamentary oversight in India, recommending clearer legal charters for RAW and IB and independent inquiry mechanisms for misuse of secret funds.

Firoze Hirjikaka's "Cornucopia" criticises political pressure on the Marathi film Jhenda and the Shiv Sena's attacks on Shah Rukh Khan, Mukesh Ambani, and Rahul Gandhi over who belongs in Mumbai, arguing private intimidation is eroding democratic freedoms.

Keshav Rau criticises Rahul Gandhi's remarks minimising the Maharashtra Police's role in the 26/11 response, arguing anti-migrant Shiv Sena/MNS politics must be resisted through firm law enforcement rather than rhetoric that alienates ordinary Maharashtrians.

M. D. Kini's obituary essay on Jyoti Basu rejects celebratory accounts of his career, crediting land reform but blaming militant trade unionism and public-sector failure for West Bengal's industrial decline and capital flight.

Ashok Karnik's "Point Counter Point" addresses attacks on Indians in Australia, Pakistan's post-26/11 evasions, and the rise of private 'enforcers' threatening films and public figures, closing with N. Vittal's contrast between Indian and Chinese freedom of expression.
Firoze Hirjikaka argues secularism in the West has curdled into reverse intolerance toward harmless religious expression, while remaining skeptical of organised religion himself.

Ram Narayanan publishes an online debate on whether India should seek accommodation with China through territorial concessions, weighted toward retired military officers and analysts warning that surrendering Tawang would invite further pressure.

Sharad Joshi's "The Liberal Dissent" explains his Rajya Sabha opposition to the Women's Reservation Bill, supporting greater women's political representation while rejecting its lottery-cum-rotation design and proposing multi-seat constituencies guaranteeing a vote for a woman candidate instead.

Meera Sanyal endorses more women MPs and MLAs but argues reservation is the wrong method, drawing on banking-sector gender-diversity practices to propose a voluntary political talent pipeline for women candidates.

Aroon Tikekar's tribute to Marathi poet Vinda Karandikar remembers his frugality, generosity, and role alongside Vasant Bapat and Mangesh Padgaonkar in popularising poetry recitation across Maharashtra, as well as his translations of King Lear and Aristotle's Poetics.

Sharad Joshi's "Maharashtra at Fifty" argues the state's golden-jubilee should be judged against the original Samyukta Maharashtra movement's aspirations, criticising the economic exploitation of Vidarbha and Marathwada, farmer distress, and the decline of genuine trade unionism.

Sethu Das compares Gandhi's Hind Swaraj with Thomas Paine's Common Sense as anti-colonial pamphlets that challenged imperial power, linking Gandhi's non-violence to Tibetan exile politics through Samdhong Rinpoche.

Ashok Karnik's "Point Counter Point" weighs the value of talks with Pakistan after 26/11, distinguishes state excesses from planned Naxalite violence, and debates whether local opposition should block the Peddar Road flyover.

A reprint section revisits April 1953 Freedom First material on communist news suppression alongside Amlan Datta's 2004 letter attributing the Left Front's long rule in West Bengal to Congress's organisational weakness and ambivalence toward the CPI(M), to whose memory the issue is dedicated.

The cover feature reports a March 2010 ICCF public discussion on "paid news," in which speakers including Jehangir Patel and Krishna Prasad argue that the sale of editorial space as advertising, disguised across politics, business, and sport, has become a systemic threat to journalism and democratic accountability.

Aroon Tikekar's "Timid Candidates, Pampered Journalists" narrows the paid-news theme to Marathi journalism, arguing that a proliferation of awards and politician-backed patronage has weakened professional independence, while voicing guarded optimism that credibility may eventually recover.

P. M. Kamath defends Maharashtra's proposed offshore Shivaji statue against criticism that it wastes public resources, reframing it as both a tourism asset and a post-26/11 coastal security and intelligence platform.

Amit Dholakia's "Gujarat at 50: An Introspective Look" presents Gujarat as a paradox of economic dynamism and entrepreneurial energy alongside communal polarisation, weak social indicators, and constricted dissent under Modi-centred politics.
R. C. Saxena's companion piece on Gujarat at fifty distinguishes prosperity from liberal modernity, framing itself as a skeptical response to celebratory development statistics.

Ashok Karnik's "Point Counter Point" withholds judgment on US cooperation in the Headley case, criticises Congress discomfort over Amitabh Bachchan's appearance with Gujarat's chief minister, doubts Pakistan's sincerity in talks, and criticises the state's confused response to the Dantewada Maoist massacre.

R. Srinivasan's memorial note for Professor Amrik Singh remembers him as a major figure in Indian higher education and a longtime associate of the Indian Committee for Cultural Freedom and Indian Liberal Group.

Christie Davies argues every major actor lost Britain's 2010 general election, blaming Labour for fiscal and regulatory failure, criticising the Liberal Democrats' unstable coalition with the Conservatives, and portraying British party leaders as remote, public-school elites.

The 35th-anniversary Emergency feature recalls the 1975 declaration through Minoo Masani's account and reprints A. D. Gorwala's 1976 record of the suppression of his journal Opinion, describing censorship, forfeiture threats, and postal obstruction as incompatible with an editor's duty.

Firoze Hirjikaka's "The Great IPL Circus" follows Lalit Modi, Shashi Tharoor, Sunanda Pushkar, and Sharad Pawar through the 2010 IPL scandal, arguing it revealed how public power, private enrichment, and celebrity culture overlapped.

Ashok Karnik's "Point Counter Point" debates the Lalit Modi/Tharoor affair, criticises Arundhati Roy's defence of Maoist violence, and weighs reformative criminal justice against capital punishment in the Ajmal Kasab death-sentence debate.

Eustace D'Souza's agenda for the new Chief of the Army Staff calls for a Chief of Defence Staff, modernised equipment, urgent officer-shortage remedies, and stronger representation of military expertise in government, arguing the Sukna controversy should not distract from deeper institutional problems.

Suresh C. Sharma argues the Army should not be deployed against India's own people except for aid to civil power, drawing on the Telangana, Nagaland, Mizoram, Kashmir, and Punjab insurgencies to warn that Army involvement in domestic intelligence would damage democratic values, against a counter-view calling for specially trained paramilitary forces against the Maoists.

Ali Khwaja's "Why I Have Never Voted" explains his abstention through Bangalore municipal-election experience of intimidating canvassing, cash distribution, and winners taking office with less than half the votes cast.

Firoze Hirjikaka's "What To Do About Pakistan" argues India must find concrete ways to impose costs on Pakistan rather than fixating symbolically on Hafiz Saeed, and a closing excerpt reports Nepal's Maoists calling off an indefinite Kathmandu strike after governing worse than the politicians voters had rejected in 2008.

Keshav Rau argues India's reaction to the delayed 2010 Bhopal verdict follows a familiar pattern of outrage, media theatre, and calls for reform followed by inaction, questioning whether arresting Warren Anderson would materially aid victims still lacking relief and site cleanup.

K. Subramanian's technical account describes the Bhopal disaster as preventable, tracing Union Carbide's market miscalculation, cost-cutting on safety systems, and ignored engineering warnings stretching back years before the leak.

Firoze Hirjikaka and Nitin Raut both defend Israel over the Gaza flotilla raid, with Hirjikaka arguing Israel is strategically secure but politically inept at managing international opinion and Raut casting the Mavi Marmara voyage as a Turkish political move rather than a humanitarian mission.

H. R. Bapu Satyanarayana argues Maoist attacks including the Howrah-Mumbai train incident expose the UPA government's lack of a coherent security policy, wrestling with the dilemma that force may harm tribal civilians while inaction leaves the state looking helpless.
Aroon Tikekar's memorial profile of G. P. Pradhan presents him as a Gandhian teacher-politician whose ethical, secular liberalism drew on Ranade, Gokhale, Tilak, Phule, and Ambedkar.

Ashok Karnik's "Point Counter Point" is skeptical of caste enumeration in the 2011 census as deepening concessions politics, and questions confusion over Home Minister Chidambaram's 'limited mandate' against Naxalism.

Sadanand B. Kumta cites a Hong Kong-based survey ranking India last among twelve Asian bureaucracies, arguing public servants have become masters rather than servants and defending RTI transparency against proposed exclusions.

An archival reprint of P. Kodanda Rao's 1953 essay argues language has no nationality and should be judged by communicational utility, rejecting the idea that English is inherently foreign to Indians.

Nitin Raut argues the July 2010 India-Pakistan foreign-ministerial talks were damaging for India because Pakistan had not acted against terrorism and could exploit dialogue to deflect attention, urging stronger internal security instead.

P. M. Kamath, via a reprinted K. P. Sreenivasan column and his own piece, argues Pakistan has leveraged its strategic usefulness to the US into rewards while continuing to shelter militant groups, framing its demand for a civil nuclear deal as an insistence on parity with India.

Ashok Karnik's "Point Counter Point" weighs Bhopal justice against the limits of criminal punishment, contrasts India's desire for access to David Headley with US plea-bargaining realities, and questions whether the government can distinguish between the Afzal Guru and Kasab mercy petitions.
Meera Sanyal compares Indian and American democracy after the Times Square bomb case, arguing India can learn from clearer governmental accountability and citizen ownership under 'We the people.'

Jyoti Marwah reports on a national seminar, "My Country India: Reviving Patriotism of 1885," aiming to reconnect civic memory with India's anti-colonial and diverse past rather than empty nationalist symbolism.

Keshav Rau critiques the Group of Ministers' recommendations on Bhopal as politically useful but substantively thin, arguing proposed compensation is undercut by disputed casualty classifications and doubting the belated push to extradite Warren Anderson.

Salil Tripathi compares the BP oil spill response with Bhopal to argue that home governments and corporations owe victims accountability beyond borders, contrasting Obama's aggressive BP response with US closure-seeking over Bhopal.
R. Srinivasan's tribute to sociologist Dr. Dhirendra Narain remembers him as a beloved Mumbai University teacher known for courtesy and scholarly generosity.

Ashok Karnik's article on the XIX Commonwealth Games argues that allegations of mismanagement and corruption are serious but urges readers not to let media spectacle and political score-settling undermine the Games before they occur, comparing India's anxieties to South Africa's pre-World Cup doubts.

Firoze Hirjikaka reads the WikiLeaks Afghanistan documents as evidence the United States knowingly tolerated Pakistan's double game of receiving aid while its intelligence networks aided the Taliban and Al Qaeda, concluding that expediency governs both war and politics.

Neelakant Patri criticises Sharad Pawar's food ministry for failing to protect consumers from rising food prices, blaming administrative failures, hoarding, and poor storage rather than natural scarcity.

M. B. Damania uses the Bhopal/Union Carbide controversy to question the public appetite for scapegoats, contrasting Satish Dhawan's handling of an ISRO failure with demands for punishment after Bhopal and arguing accountability should distinguish negligence from criminal intent.

Vinay Hardikar's tribute to S. H. Deshpande presents him as a Marathi liberal economist and public intellectual who connected Hindutva, democracy, and social development without becoming a partisan ideologue.
Sharad Bailur opposes a proposed salary hike for Members of Parliament, arguing for a transparent, market-valued compensation package stripped of hidden perks rather than raising salaries alone.
A tribute to novelist and liberal candidate Manohar Malgonkar accompanies a reprinted 1964 article defending the constitutional promises made to Indian princes against the abolition of privy purses.

Ashok Karnik's "Point Counter Point" weighs scientific versus customary claims about khap panchayat authority over gotra marriage rules, and debates whether television coverage of communal violence amplifies political hooliganism.

The editor's note states Freedom First's position on Kashmir: the wishes of the people of Jammu and Kashmir should be ascertained, but law and order and the end of terrorism are preconditions for any next step.

The Kashmir cover feature, based on a Mumbai seminar, presents Ashok Karnik's argument that separatist demands escalate with each concession, that 'azaadi' rather than unemployment is the agitators' real demand, and that India should restore control and 'wait it out' rather than seek a quick settlement, warning that plebiscite logic could revive the two-nation theory.

Firoze Hirjikaka's intervention in the Kashmir seminar challenges conventional wisdom by suggesting India might let the Valley go or use that possibility to negotiate from strength, while V. Balachandran distinguishes externally sponsored insurgency from domestic law-and-order problems and criticises media overexposure of Kashmir compared with Manipur.

Eustace D'Souza's account of his 2010 visit to the North East rejects alarmist claims of poor Army morale and equipment scarcity, describing effective road development, schools, and interreligious integration in units stationed in Arunachal Pradesh and Manipur.

Memorial tributes remember businessman and philanthropist Jamshed N. Guzder and political science teacher Professor Aloo J. Dastur, an opponent of the Emergency and champion of minority rights and secular liberalism.

Reader letters reject the idea that Commonwealth Games prestige should suppress corruption allegations, arguing national prestige depends more on reducing poverty and illiteracy than on expensive spectacles.

Ram Narayanan's column collects an email exchange between Mahendra Dave and Irfan Hussain contrasting Pakistan's religious-state politics with India's secular framework, alongside an Afghan national security adviser's excerpt on the need for clarity about state sponsors of terrorism.

Firoze Hirjikaka's cover essay "Vandalizing India's Democracy" argues Indians have let elected representatives behave like rulers rather than servants, tracing municipal corruption and Commonwealth Games mismanagement to citizen apathy and electoral disengagement, and calls for mass political communication rather than elite commentary alone.

Ashok Karnik's "Crisis of Governance" portrays the UPA-II government as trapped in indecision through Groups of Ministers and prime-ministerial hesitation, surveying inflation, Naxalism, Kashmir, China, and the Commonwealth Games as symptoms of an absence of authority and accountability.

Furdoon S. B. Mehta, drawing on Maja Daruwala's police-reform work, argues public order cannot be separated from rights, transparency, and accountable policing, criticising states and the Centre for evading Supreme Court directions on police reform.

N. Vittal begins a three-part serial on "Accountability in Public Service," proposing the equation output equals input times accountability and contrasting citizens in democratic states with subjects in totalitarian regimes.

Sanjeev Sabhlok's "India Needs a Non-Interfering Agriculture Policy" argues food security depends on property rights and open markets, attacking the Essential Commodities Act, procurement, and PDS corruption while calling for people support rather than price support.

Ashok Karnik's "Point Counter Point" criticises Salman Khan for minimising responsibility for 26/11, treats the Jama Masjid attack as evidence terrorism had returned to Delhi, and describes the Ayodhya verdict as legally imperfect but politically useful for settlement.

The editor's note frames the Bihar Assembly election as a possible test of whether Indians behave as assertive citizens or subservient subjects, continuing the magazine's Kashmir coverage and inviting reader responses.

The editor's note welcomes Aung San Suu Kyi's release from detention as a standard against which Indian public life appears lacking in moral courage, framing the issue around the Adarsh scandal and broader corruption.

Christie Davies compares British and Indian political inheritance, arguing Britain suffers from interlocking elite cliques but not kinship-based rule, while India has repeatedly converted charisma and bereavement into dynastic succession from Indira Gandhi through Sonia and Rahul Gandhi.

Ashok Karnik's cover essay asks why India is so corrupt, using Transparency International rankings and contrasting China's punishment of corrupt officials with India's procedural delay, connecting Bhopal, the Commonwealth Games, and Adarsh as evidence that bribery has been normalised from the traffic constable up.

Firoze Hirjikaka reads the Adarsh Housing Society scandal as proof of an entrenched postcolonial 'mai-baap sarkar' mentality, but credits the Right to Information Act and independent television with beginning to force officials to explain themselves.

N. Vittal's second installment on "Accountability in Public Service" identifies institutional weaknesses including Article 311 protections and inflated confidential reports, proposing transparency, e-governance, and process redesign as remedies.

Ashok Karnik's "Point Counter Point" takes a skeptical view of Pervez Musharraf's return to Pakistani politics and Omar Abdullah's accession-versus-merger rhetoric on Kashmir, while V. Balachandran separately questions what Kashmir interlocutors can contribute beyond existing Track-II dialogues.

Firoze Hirjikaka's "Cornucopia" criticises Mumbai's over-securing of South Bombay during President Obama's visit and condemns the Shiv Sena's intimidation campaign against Rohinton Mistry's Such a Long Journey as stale politics unsuited to a smarter electorate.

A retrospective page reprints December 1953 Freedom First material including Narie Oliaji's essay against subordinating art to political uplift and a note on press liberty following a Calcutta clash between newspapermen and police.

The editor's New Year note frames the issue around the 2G spectrum scandal and parliamentary paralysis, previewing essays on liberal personalities including Ram Manohar Lohia, C. Rajagopalachari, and Nani Palkhivala.

Firoze Hirjikaka's "Dumb Charades In Parliament" argues Congress and BJP theatrics over a Joint Parliamentary Committee are a staged distraction, since genuine anti-corruption reform would require limiting the ministerial and bureaucratic discretion both parties benefit from.

Sharad Bailur argues the opposition's demand for a JPC into the 2G scandal is inadequate unless paired with a Supreme Court-supervised CBI investigation, criticising coalition politics for giving small regional parties disproportionate leverage.

A. D. Gorwala's reprinted essay asks whether bribery has become so normalised in India that it is treated as ordinary social behaviour, arguing corruption grew after Independence as older standards of public service collapsed.

Nagesh Kini and M. B. Damania both examine everyday corruption, with Kini calling for civic self-scrutiny against complicity in forged certificates and voter apathy, and Damania describing how officials extract bribes through procedural delay and implied threats without ever naming a sum.

Subhash Athale argues India's first-past-the-post electoral system fosters corruption by making elections prohibitively expensive, proposing proportional and preferential voting along with campaign-finance reform and abolition of high-value cash notes as remedies.

Sadanand B. Kumta reads India's 2010 Human Development Index rank of 119 among 169 countries as evidence growth has not translated into comparable gains in health, education, and nutrition, comparing India unfavourably with China, Sri Lanka, and Bangladesh.

Ashok Karnik's "Point Counter Point" judges President Obama's India visit a diplomatic success despite criticism over Pakistan and outsourcing, and treats the Adarsh scandal as elite manipulation of land rules while warning that anti-corruption zeal must preserve due process.

N. Vittal concludes his three-part "Accountability in Public Service" series by summarising New Public Management proposals such as fixed-term chief executives and professionalised agencies, expressing optimism about Indian democracy's self-correcting mechanisms.
